Title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-shirudo

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/introducing-shirudo/

Markdown Content:
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a [controlled test⁠(opens in a new window)](https://isovalent.com/blog/post/cisco-openai-shirudo/), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

## How Shirudo works

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:

*   **Live protection:** eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

*   **Defense at machine speed:** OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

*   **Trusted deployment:** Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

*   **Hardware-backed verification:** Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

The [Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window)](https://lpc.events/event/20/contributions/2437/) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to [apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4v2xA_NJHt0). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more [here⁠(opens in a new window)](https://isovalent.com/blog/post/cisco-openai-shirudo/).

## Rethinking infrastructure

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

## Building in the open

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing[Shirudo⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

*   **Try Shirudo:** Follow the[VM quickstart⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.shirudo.dev/start/quickstart.html) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

*   **Get hands-on:** Explore Shirudo through [Isovalent's self-guided lab⁠(opens in a new window)](https://labs.isovalent.com/#/lab/shirudo-getting-started).

*   **Join the technical deep dive:** Register for the [December 15 webinar⁠(opens in a new window)](https://isovalent.site/4t8Pjxc).

We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the[code on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo), read the[docs⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.shirudo.dev/index.html), and[let us know what you find⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.shirudo.dev/contribute/support.html).

Title: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days

URL Source: https://openai.com/business/customer-stories/richpanel-ai-customer-support

Final URL: https://openai.com/business/customer-stories/richpanel-ai-customer-support/

Markdown Content:
Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions.

According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down.

[Richpanel⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.richpanel.com/) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations.

> _“The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.”_

—Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel

## Building the tools and procedures for AI support

Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?”

So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need.

Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow.

## Balancing intelligence and cost across support operations

Richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an important part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents.

“What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point.

Amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow.

> “OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient.”

—Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel

At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months.

The company guarantees customers a 50% automation rate within the first 30 days or their money back. Amit says it met that commitment across all of those deployments, adding, “In each of the cases, the AI is beating human support agents when it comes to customer satisfaction.”

# Merry Making: Play, Build and Create With NVIDIA Technologies This Holiday Season

 Get into the game, bring a creative project to life or try building a robot with NVIDIA platforms.

November 23, 2026 by[NVIDIA Writers](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/nvidiawriters/ "Posts by NVIDIA Writers")

The elves don’t have to be the only ones busy in the workshop this holiday season. With the lights twinkling and the gift wrap out, it’s the perfect time to give someone — or yourself — a spark to take a hobby to the next level.

For some, that means diving into a new game. For others, it’s video editing or even building a robot.

NVIDIA technologies offer something for everyone on Santa’s list. Read on to unwrap the details.

## **Make Time for One More Game**

With the holiday break here, everyone can be online to score bragging rights or explore a world that’s only been seen in video game trailers.

For some players, an upgrade means a desktop that brings out the detail in every scene. For others, it’s a laptop they can take along when visiting family, or a way to play in the cloud on a device they already own.

The right setup depends on where and what to play:

*   [GeForce RTX 50 Series](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/graphics-cards/50-series/) laptops and desktops power the action. Built on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, they feature fifth-generation Tensor Cores and fourth-generation RT Cores for AI-enhanced graphics, detailed ray-traced worlds and high frames-per-second gaming.
*   [NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/) combine RTX graphics with NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform on a single superchip, bringing decades of NVIDIA innovation to slim, premium laptops and compact desktops on the familiar Windows platform. One PC can handle every workflow, from accelerated creation and immersive gaming to powerful local AI — with a variety of designs and all-day battery life.
*   See games in a new light with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology, which boosts performance and enhances image quality. The newest feature, DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, infuses scenes with lifelike lighting and materials in supported games. [Get a glimpse of _NBA 2K27_ with DLSS 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LHUzFnq70b8).
*   NVIDIA Reflex and G-SYNC make gameplay more responsive and fluid. Reflex reduces system latency in supported games, while [G-SYNC displays](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/products/g-sync-monitors/) use variable refresh rates to deliver smooth, tear-free gaming.
*   The [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/) cloud gaming service enables playing top titles anywhere. Stream supported games on compatible laptops, TVs, handhelds and more. Connect to supported game stores to play owned PC games, with more than 4,500 titles available across the service.

## **Make Something Worth Sharing**

For creators with a project that’s been on the backburner, the right gift this season can be the push to finally make it happen. Maybe it’s holiday clips becoming a short film, a snowy scene coming together in 3D or a livestream that brings friends across time zones to the same virtual table. Creators can use NVIDIA systems — such as GeForce RTX 50 Series and RTX Spark devices — to keep up with the workflows, along with [NVIDIA Studio tools](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/studio/) and technologies for AI acceleration.

Studio Drivers support video editing, 3D design and livestreaming. In supported applications, faster processing gives more room to experiment and refine.

## **Build a Robot That Thinks**

Every robot starts somewhere. This season, it could be under the tree.

Building a robot is an experiment in teaching a device to see or sense its surroundings. A first project might be as simple as using a camera to identify a candy cane or a gingerbread man, then moving on to an app that probes what the camera sees.

Testing brings new questions. Can the robot recognize the candy cane under twinkling lights? Can it tell a frosted gingerbread man from an unfrosted one? Each experiment leaves more to improve and explore.

The NVIDIA Jetson edge AI platform provides the hardware and software to build projects like these. It combines compact computers with the [NVIDIA JetPack](https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded/jetpack) software development kit to help makers build robots, autonomous machines and intelligent devices.

A [Jetson Developer Kit](https://marketplace.nvidia.com/robotics-edge/) is a gift to explore computer vision, generative AI and multimodal robot control, with the option to add cameras and sensors suited to various projects. AI runs directly on the device, processing information from its surroundings. When ready to take a prototype further, production systems powered by Jetson modules provide a path to deployment.

With Hermes Agent and NVIDIA Cosmos, developers can explore how AI connects everyday requests with actions in the physical world.

Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company
announced
the launch of
Claude Ship
, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.
The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.
Image Credits:
Anthropic
The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.
“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”
Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.
The new offering consists of Code Review, which is
already generally available

Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.

articles.content:
AI investing startup
Supertake
has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.
Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including
Nat Friedman
, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.
Michael Mignano
originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.
Image Credits:
Supertake
“We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.
The team includes co-founders
Lincoln Murr
(CEO) and
John Peterson
(CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.
The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.
Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.
Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.
Image Credits:
Supertake
Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.
For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.
Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.
Image Credits:
Supertake example (screenshot)
“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he says. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”
“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.
Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.
“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being said, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.
Image Credits:
Screenshot
To address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team says it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.
“We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” says Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”
Access to
Supertake
is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders said they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.
Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.
With the new funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team says it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

A handful of tech CEOs, including Elon Musk, are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia. Despite being caught in three affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy that has triggered multiple congressional investigations over national security concerns —
Huang was reinstated as CEO
and president of Nvidia on Monday morning.
“The mistake has been corrected,” Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk
wrote
on X about Huang’s return.
The mistake has been corrected
https://t.co/UKvEng9rCD
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk)
November 23, 2026
Musk had been among the most vocal tech leaders to advocate for Huang.
“I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders,” Musk
said
last week at the DealBook Summit.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had taken a more neutral stance, commenting last week, “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”
Altman had experienced a similar situation when he was
ousted
as CEO of OpenAI, then reinstated days later. After the announcement that Huang would return, Altman simply posted, “Jensen!” Many other tech CEOs have similarly refrained from commenting on the matter, given the shifting politics surrounding Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, as well as the national security concerns at the center of the controversy.
Jensen!
— Sam Altman (@sama)
November 23, 2026
In addition to Musk, Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ), who served prison time for failing to stop criminal activity on the Binance crypto exchange, is also supportive of Huang.
“Glad to see @JensenHuang back,” CZ
posted
on X with a clapping hands emoji.
Glad to see
@JensenHuang
back. 👏
https://t.co/WrUjvmEyVi
— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance)
November 23, 2026
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who had been among 200,000 signatories on
an open letter
calling for Huang’s reinstatement,
wrote
on X, “Jensen’s return will be a demonstration of American resiliency to corporate, political and journalistic missteps.”
Another signatory on the open letter, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, who had similarly been
driven out of the company he founded after scandals
, also voiced his support for Huang on X.
Will have to save this for another day 😅😎
pic.twitter.com/dLqJosDpPZ

November 23, 2026
When Nvidia’s stock tanked in reaction to Huang’s ousting, billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said he believes that the Nvidia board was “not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties.” As Nvidia’s stock began to rebound Monday morning, Ackman
wrote
, “The wisdom of the crowd prevails.”
The attitude toward Huang’s return is not as celebratory outside of the tech industry.
Across the political spectrum
, some elected officials are skeptical about President Donald Trump’s
claims
that Huang’s return does not threaten national security.
“No national security risk? Based on what?”
wrote
Senator John Cornyn (R-TX).
Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking “candor.” I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.

Huang is still
expected to testify publicly
before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, as well as privately before three House committees.

Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist
Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the
alleged Chinese espionage scandal
involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor
reported
Monday.
The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes.
This list
“contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.”
Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.”
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had
launched a criminal probe
into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and
illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China
. The company has denied wrongdoing.
TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds.
After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was
reinstated as Nvidia CEO
on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang.

Nvidia employees greet Jensen Huang like a hero as he returns to company’s HQ
Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices on Monday to an applauding crowd of hundreds of employees, according to several videos circulating online.
The embattled Nvidia founder had stepped down earlier this month amid

— including an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has triggered multiple Congressional hearings over national security, and two affairs with Nvidia employees — but was reinstated as CEO after pushback from the tech community and an

After basking in chants of his name, Huang briefly addressed the crowd.

Amid this increased scrutiny, however, other reports have depicted a different side to Nvidia’s top exec — one where Jensen is not seen as a beloved leader, but as a brutal bully. articles.content:
Google
announced
on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives. The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos.
By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem. Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match. Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time.
Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards. The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money.
Image Credits:
Google
As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets. By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season.
Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa.
Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context that AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses.
The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context.

articles.content:
It’s safe to say no one expected
this
.
Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news.
Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the U.S. government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning.
Most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend,
The New York Times reported
sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.
With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating U.S. export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a company alongside Huang himself.
Then there are the questions raised by Trump’s intervention. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but
calling the Nvidia board
goes significantly further. Huang has already
donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project
, so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit.
All of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and
retains significant financial ties to the industry
through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.
If all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s
statement to CBS
, which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it.
I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang two weeks ago. Since then, the cost of removing him has gone up: an open letter from Nvidia’s employees and partners, a tanking stock market, and, ultimately, direct intervention from the president of the United States.
But nothing has lowered the cost of keeping Huang, and the ugly scenario the board foresaw earlier this month is still very much in place. We’re about to see it come to life.

A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump
reportedly
dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s
reinstatement
shortly afterward.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president
told
CNBC.
Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had
affairs
with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.
“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.
The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to
remark
that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”
According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
While Trump has
declared
that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.
“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC.
Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even
denying
that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times
reported
, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.
Earlier this spring, Rubio also
supervised
the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

articles.content:
President Trump
praised
Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk.
In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case.
There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board.
Speaking to a PBS journalist
over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.”
Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions.
Trump
said last week
that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below.
The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP

Enterprise customer experience company
Sierra
, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round that doubles the company’s valuation to $30 billion. The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which
valued the company at $15 billion
.
The new round was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors who have led previous rounds, including Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV, and Tiger Global.
Enterprise automation is among the few areas where AI has seen rapid adoption. Sierra said that it currently serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies, and its clients include BNY, HSBC, Singtel, Wells Fargo, JPMorganChase, Pearson, Next, and Cox Automotive. The company late last month said its outcome-based pricing model has helped it double its run-rate revenue to
$400 million within five months
.
That said, Sierra is working along similar lines as other customer experience players in the market, which is
creating a platform to build agents and partner
with model developers to provide choices to enterprises. As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on
creating protocol definitions
for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart.
Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals.
Startups operating in the CX space have seen multimillion-dollar rounds come their way with soaring valuations. Voice AI company ElevenLabs is now valued at $22 billion;
Decagon is valued at $4.5 billion
;
Wonderful is valued at $5 billion
; and
Parloa is valued at $3 billion
. Multiple other startups have scored investments of more than $100 million.
During the HumanX conference in Amsterdam in September, Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor argued that despite the popular belief that AI-powered CX companies are replacing humans in contact centers, a majority of its customers are reassigning roles to existing employees.

articles.content:
In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board
said
on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he
resigned
following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.
The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET.
In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.
Trump also said the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.
A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom
signed a petition
pushing for reinstatement.
The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”
Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.
“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”
In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next?

Elizabeth Lopatto
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.
I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened.
Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now.
The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy
I have argued here, in the past, that the Epstein case laid bare the real politics of the revanchist American right wing:
total elite impunity
. Well, here it is again! If you are close enough with Trump, it doesn’t matter if you may have
jeopardized national security
by fucking
an alleged Chinese spy
. You won’t even be investigated for it before the American president calls in to your board of directors’ meeting to
demand you be reinstated
. I mean, it
is
the era of
gangster tech regulation
— what were any of us expecting? The deal was reportedly brokered by
Peter Thiel’s very own boy
,
Vance
.
Just so we can be absolutely clear about what transpired at Nvidia, let’s quickly go through the facts as we know them. A Chinese citizen named
Alice Huang acquired the company she renamed Megaspeed
, the Singaporean data firm at the center of this inquiry, in 2023. At some point, Huang met Huang, and the two were seen together at a dinner that December. From 2024 to 2025, Megaspeed received more than 200 Nvidia shipments.
In September 2025, the US government began investigating Megaspeed for possible violations of chip export controls; that October, the State Department told Trump of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, who was described as a Chinese intelligence asset. Also in October,
The New York Times
first reported on Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia
. In December, Trump — who has a close relationship with Jensen Huang — allowed Nvidia to sell more powerful chips to China. In March 2026, Marco Rubio warned the government about Alice, and Trump nonetheless invited Huang to a visit in China. In October,
The New York Times
reported on the affair. Shortly after Huang sent
a note to Nvidia admitting to it
, several other reports of infidelity — this time with Nvidia employees — surfaced. On November 12th, Huang resigned. On November 17th, during the Nvidia earnings call, the board’s chair said that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On November 23rd, Huang was back.
This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive
What changed between last week and this week? A week was not enough time to truly review all the information on Huang and his paramour, Alice “No Relation” Huang, the international woman of mystery. The explanation seems to be that Nvidia’s board succumbed to a pressure campaign from Huang’s fellow billionaires, and
a direct intervention from the president and vice president of the United States of America
.
Sure, all these CEOs ostensibly wanted Huang back at Nvidia to keep the AI trade going. Still, watching the likes of Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, investing loudmouth Bill Ackman, and Elon Musk — who actually
did
appear in the Epstein files, and who seemed to be pretty friendly with Epstein! — pitch a fit last week was instructive. These men worried that they might be punished for wrongdoing, that they did not get big enough to be above the law. They have now been reassured, and I suppose that is what really matters. After all, Trump said on CNBC that he gave Nvidia’s board assurances that Jensen is “
absolutely fine
.”
This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive, and not just because Huang is CEO of Nvidia again. Almost in passing, Trump noted that he had “protected” Musk in his first term from “a certain incident [that] took place, a very tough incident.” In his own inimitable style,
Trump told Jim Cramer
, “You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally.
Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally
One thing that has perhaps emboldened this crew is the stance
from professional politics-knowers
— and
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries
— that
holding members of the Trump administration accountable
might be a
hindrance to governing
. That
accountability was part of the reason
for
the blue wave
in November seems to have bypassed these pundits (and the presumptive House majority leader). But then, why should we believe that Democrats will thoroughly investigate this? Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is
claiming to want
an investigation, but I am skeptical of how deep that investigation will go as long as Schumer leads it, and only partially because he’s been
allied with Silicon Valley for more than a decade
. He also
has a daughter who works at OpenAI
, a company that Nvidia invests in and that is dependent on Nvidia chips. How hard is he really willing to go?
Of course, there may be more to this than just pure economic self-interest. In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump posted a remarkable image. It is an altered picture of Trump himself, taken after a failed assassination attempt in 2024. Trump’s head has been replaced with Jensen Huang’s head. The American flag has been replaced with the Nvidia logo. Huang is waving a bright red bra. It seems I owe Sigmund Freud an apology. In the end, these men fear nothing more than losing power for sexual shenanigans — and
especially
losing power to a woman.
Leave aside the national security issues for a minute and focus on the two Nvidia employees. Dating subordinates is a serious conflict of interest; the
CEO of Nestle lost his job for just that last year
. This is a major violation for CEOs of normal companies, but it is common practice among the sleazeballs of Silicon Valley:
Bill Gates is famous for it
and it was
plainly rampant
at Google,
a tone set by
Sergey Brin himself
. I am sure that you will be shocked, shocked to discover that in the wake of MeToo, Brin was among the men who
suddenly swung right
. I mean, Musk himself announced
he was a Republican the day before
Business Insider
reported that
he exposed himself to a flight attendant and paid hush money to cover it up
.
If you’re rich enough, and connected enough, everything is permitted
The Republican Party has made the abuse of women without consequences one of its main issues; that the lesser violation of sleeping with subordinates would also be something the revanchists would defend seems obvious. That was clear from the botched investigation of the Epstein affair itself, the botched release of the Epstein files, and the assorted confirmation hearings of
Pete Hegseth
,
Brett Kavanaugh
, and
Todd Blanche
. (To say nothing of the
Andrew Tate business
.) But in all this, let’s not forget that Trump has been accused of sexual misconduct by
no fewer than 28 women
. So I’m sure it was an affront to all these guys that not only did Huang’s misconduct include a series of affairs, but he was also replaced by Colette Kress, who is known to be a woman.
I suppose we might as well pass by
the various
reports that Huang
allegedly terrorized
his employees. In light of everything else, this seems minor by comparison.
Anyway I had that all in mind when I saw Epic’s Sweeney celebrating the state intrusion into theoretically private companies by
posting “Back in Black,”
an oblique reference to Huang’s leather jackets that is also from the later, lesser period of AC/DC, after Bon Scott died and AC/DC became an AC/DC tribute band. He also called
The New York Times
’ reporting into Huang “lies.”
Musk continued his streak of
Sephiroth posting
: “
The mistake has been corrected
.” Jason Calacanis, the
All-In
podcast’s village idiot, posted, “
GPU Jesus has risen!
” along with an openly blasphemous, AI-generated image of Huang as Christ.
Best of luck to Joon Kim, the Wachtell Lipton partner and former federal prosecutor who is conducting “
a thorough and independent investigation
” into Huang’s alleged misconduct on behalf of Nvidia’s board. I assume Kim has, like the rest of us, gotten the message loud and clear: If you’re rich enough, and connected enough, everything is permitted. Or perhaps, more succinctly: lol nothing
matters.

Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.
Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced
in March
and became generally available
in October
. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.
PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.
Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next?

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and
that he
“created problems for the board.”
Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from
The New York Times
said
he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency
had enlisted
that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was
under investigation
for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell.
So when Huang resigned less than two weeks ago, the decision seemed final. Even Nvidia’s board appeared unwilling to budge. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones
said during an earnings call last week
.
But in the days following Huang’s resignation, the founder’s allies — including President Donald Trump — mounted a pressure campaign that brought him back to the company he created and sent Nvidia’s share price rocketing upward, almost as though he had never left.
The campaign in support of Huang began almost immediately after his resignation. A coterie of tech leaders
began posting in support
of Nvidia’s founder: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney
questioned
the motives of journalists who broke the stories about his affairs. Tesla CEO Elon Musk likened Huang’s
departure
to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later said on stage
, “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.”
“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
— Donald Trump
Meanwhile, some of those tech leaders began questioning aspects of the reporting that led to Huang’s exit.
Venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks
cast doubt that Alice Huang was a spy, citing a lack of confirmation from US officials. Trump exacerbated the uncertainty,
telling reporters
, “I don’t know that she is a spy,” despite reports saying the assessment had
relied on
US intelligence sources.
Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, found itself in a tough position. The company’s
shares crashed
following Huang’s departure, and they didn’t pick up even after a rosy earnings report. The board was also scrambling to find a new CEO,
something industry analysts speculated
would
prove exceptionally difficult
. Reports indicated that Nvidia was considering
hiring Arm CEO Rene Haas
and Apple hardware
chief Johny Srouji
, both of whom already have powerful roles in the chip industry.
Trump quickly warmed up to Huang’s return, too. The president — whose investment accounts
traded up to $97 million worth of Nvidia stock
since returning to office — initially floated the idea of having
former Apple CEO Tim Cook take Huang’s place
, before
saying that it
“certainly isn’t a bad idea” to bring Huang back.
This past weekend, Trump appears to have inserted himself into the situation directly. A
report from
The New York Times
says
that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and Nvidia’s board to “resolve the situation,” while the Trump administration reassured the board that it “did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.”
Semafor
reports
that Trump even called in to Nvidia’s board meeting to advocate for Huang’s reinstatement. Sunday evening, Trump
said
in a post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia’s board “rehires Jensen Huang.”
Hours later, Nvidia’s board did just that. The board announced on Monday that it
reinstated Huang as its CEO
, president, and board member. In its statement, the board said that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s reinstatement, with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung saying the president “was totally involved” in the decision. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said during an interview with CNBC. He
added in a post on
Truth Social that the US attorney general confirmed that it doesn’t have evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
Related
White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
Nvidia’s shares rose
on the news of Huang’s reinstatement, while
tech leaders celebrated his return on social media
. But the saga is likely far from over. The board said it will finish its investigation into Huang, the Securities and Exchange Commission is
looking into Nvidia’s
“accounting practices,” and Megaspeed is
being investigated
by the Justice Department. Even Trump has said that Nvidia should continue its internal investigation about export controls compliance.
Trump’s apparent involvement also leaves plenty of room for scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers,
who will control
the House and Senate next year. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA)
called
Nvidia’s decision “reckless” and urged the Trump administration to explain the “input” government officials provided to the company’s board.
Huang’s stunning reinstatement still leaves many questions unanswered. Even though the backing of Wall Street, the White House, and Silicon Valley may have brought Huang back as CEO, a new wave of scrutiny from federal regulators and lawmakers is just getting started.

articles.content:
Title: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

URL Source: https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.4

Markdown Content:
Over the past three months, we have aggressively scaled both loop depth and model size in parallel. The first surprise came from the **Loop Transformer** architecture itself. By executing a shared block of layers across multiple iterations, the model can reason more deeply without adding parameters, effectively matching the performance of much larger models.

*   **GLM-5.4** is our first flagship model built on the Loop Transformer architecture, reaching intelligence levels comparable to 2T-3T parameter models.

*   **GLM-5.4** marks the start of **Generalized Coding**, where code becomes the foundation for solving a much wider range of tasks and unlocking new capabilities.

The model still has some limitations. Most notably, it tends to get caught in overly long "marathon thinking" loops, though this prolonged reflection and self-correction does consistently improve accuracy beyond its parameter count.

## The Loop Architecture

As we noted in our GLM-5.3 technical blog, memory-intensive tasks benefit from more parameters, while reasoning-intensive tasks benefit from more effective compute. Large-scale software engineering, cybersecurity, 3D modeling, and physical control are all ultra-long-chain reasoning tasks. The model must follow multi-step causal chains while maintaining global logical consistency. Stacking parameters and memorizing data cannot solve this.

## From Pre-Trained Base to Loop Transformer

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

The idea is not new. The 2018 Universal Transformer proposed weight-shared depth, and recent work on recurrent depth and looped language models has shown gains at small scales. However, while weight sharing improves parameter efficiency, looped models trained from scratch still lag behind unshared models under the same pre-training compute budget. Instead of pre-training from scratch, we adapted an already pre-trained base model into a Loop Transformer through continued training. This lets us raise the intelligence ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead.

## Architectural Modifications at 750B Scale

GLM-5.4 loops 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for two iterations. To balance performance gains with deployment costs at the 750B scale, we made three changes after extensive experimentation:

#### **Gated Progressive Updates**

When converting middle layers of an existing model into a multi-pass loop, directly overwriting hidden states causes activation norms to blow up across iterations. Downstream layers then receive representations outside their expected scale and distribution.

GLM-5.4 adds independent per-token gates for each iteration to proportionally write candidate updates back into the residual stream. After training, these gates develop a clear division of labor. The first pass builds global context and writes conservatively with small gate values to keep scales stable. The second pass reuses this state to refine the output, opening the gates to write full updates. The gates also adjust step size dynamically based on token difficulty: on harder tokens, the first pass writes more aggressively so complex predictions benefit more from iterative refinement.

#### **Hybrid KV Cache (Global Sharing + Independent Sliding Window)**

A naive implementation keeps a full KV cache for every loop iteration, multiplying memory usage with the loop count. Instead, we build on cross-loop KV sharing by supplementing it with a local sliding window for the new pass: the second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in the first pass, while retaining its own newly generated KV within the sliding window. These two KV streams can overlap at the same positions, allowing the model to attend to both the first-pass context representations and the updated local representations from the second pass.

As a result, an extra loop only costs one sliding window of KV cache rather than a full context cache. At 1M context lengths, this keeps GLM-5.4’s deployment cost increase over GLM-5.3 well under control.

#### **Sparse Attention Index Reuse**

GLM-5.4’s base model uses sparse attention. The second loop directly reuses the attention indices generated by the first loop's indexer, adding zero indexing overhead. Our experiments show this performs nearly identically to recomputing indices on every pass.

## Scaling Correctness & Controlled Iso-Parameter Ablations

Looping is also a strict test of **Scaling Correctness**: any architectural change must still work at scale. Before committing our flagship model to it, we validated the Loop architecture progressively across 1B, 4B, 30B, and 750B base models.

On a 30B model with the exact same architecture as our 750B base, we ran a controlled iso-parameter comparison. With identical parameter counts and only ~10% more total training compute, the looped version showed clear gains:

_(Evaluated on the 30B model after 200K long-context SFT, with thinking mode enabled.)_

Two findings stand out:

*   **Longer reasoning chains benefit more.** The largest gains show up in math, scientific reasoning, and long-context tasks, which are core to Generalized Coding.

*   **Fewer tokens spent on thinking.** Across most benchmarks like GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro, average output length drops by 10–14%, mostly from shorter chains of thought. In effect, part of the reasoning shifts from explicit output tokens into the implicit depth of the loop.

## Inference Efficiency

GLM-5.4 reaches up to **200 tokens/s** during off-peak hours and maintains **70–80 tokens/s** at peak load. Achieving this throughput with a multi-pass Loop architecture required close co-design between the model and our inference infrastructure. Alongside the memory and retrieval savings from our KV cache and sparse index designs, we fused core kernels at the systems level to cut down intermediate memory reads and writes, eliminating the fragmented overhead amplified by looping.

## Generalized Coding

Coding has become the foundation for extending model capabilities. Since going all-in on coding in early 2025, we have unlocked Agentic Engineering, Long-Horizon Tasks, and Cybersecurity. Now we are pushing toward **Generalized Coding**. It has a higher ceiling and broader impact, and GLM-5.4 is just the starting point.

Driven by improvements in both coding and vision, GLM-5.4 generalizes well beyond traditional software development. It can write code to generate and edit videos, build complete games, and handle 3D modeling and mechanical design:

*   **Scaling Coding to Video:** Producing _"Hello World,"_ GLM-5.4’s self-narrated music video.

*   **Scaling Coding to Engineering:** Building a 6-axis robotic arm through engineering-grade CAD modeling in FreeCAD.

[Video 10](https://z-ai-bj.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com/prompts-rich-media-resources/5.4-blog/1517_1795370530(%E5%8E%9F%E8%A7%86%E9%A2%91).mp4)
*   **Scaling Coding to Games:** Creating a complete game directly, covering character movement, physics, maps, combat systems, and art assets.

*   **Scaling Coding to 3D:** Generating an interactive 3D macro bird-watching experience from scratch using pure mathematical geometry and custom GLSL shaders.

## Getting Started

Better performance, higher speed, and more generous usage quotas make GLM-5.4 practical for daily work. Try it here:

*   **GLM Coding Plan:**[https://z.ai/subscribe](https://z.ai/subscribe)

*   **ZCode:**[https://zcode.z.ai/en](https://zcode.z.ai/en)

*   **Z.ai Chat:**[https://chat.z.ai](https://chat.z.ai/)

*   **API (Coming Soon):**[https://z.ai/model-api](https://z.ai/model-api)

*   **Open Weights:** We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening.

## Looking Ahead

GLM-5.4 is our first step with looped architectures, and several questions remain open. We are exploring how to achieve adaptive compute so harder tokens dynamically get more iterations, and how the returns of looping behave as both loop count and model size keep growing.

We are not choosing between scaling depth and scaling model size; we are pursuing both. GLM-5.4 validates computational depth, and our next, significantly larger model will carry forward everything we learned here. It will be ready soon.

Title: How should an LLM see a computer

URL Source: https://www.greptile.com/blog/trex-computer-use

Published Time: 2026-11-19

Markdown Content:
Claude Code and Codex can both use your computer. Under the hood they work in a similar manner: both can give the model a screenshot and an accessibility tree, a text description of every button on screen, and let it click by position or by naming an element.

The text version of the screen was built decades ago, for people who couldn’t see it. In 1984, two IBM mathematicians, Jim Thatcher and his former thesis adviser, Jesse Wright, who was blind, started a side project to read the PC’s screen out loud. When GUIs turned the screen into pixels, apps had to start describing themselves instead. Microsoft shipped Active Accessibility in 1997, Sun started AT-SPI for Linux in 2001, and Apple added its Accessibility API in 2002.

This text has been useful for agents too. On the 2024 [OSWorld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07972) benchmark, models looking only at screenshots completed about one task in twenty, whereas most models reading the screen as text performed better.

How do those results hold up with stronger models? We tested screenshots on their own and with the accessibility tree on seven models, and used the results to decide how our QA agent, TREX, should see the screen.

A person clicks a button by moving the mouse to it. A model, on the other hand, looks at a screenshot and has to write the coordinates out as text (e.g., ‘x=523, y=217’) before clicking on it. Getting these numbers off by a few pixels can mean it clicks the wrong thing.

The same button sits at different coordinates on different screen and window sizes, so the guesses get worse when the resolution changes.

Also, the model’s vision works against it as it doesn’t see a screenshot pixel by pixel. The image is initially shrunk to fit the model's size limit, then cut into tiny squares, each dozens of pixels wide. But a click still has to land on one exact pixel.

Small targets are hard. On [ScreenSpot-Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07981), a 2025 benchmark with tiny targets on high resolution screens, the best model at release hit the right target only 18.9% of the time. [Anthropic’s own docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool) warn that Claude “might make mistakes or hallucinate when outputting specific coordinates.”

When [OSWorld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07972) came out in 2024, human testers were able to complete 72% of its tasks, and the best model about 12%. The authors found that models struggled with two things: turning ‘click Save’ into the right point on the screen, and knowing how to operate the software.

The first problem has a seemingly obvious fix. The accessibility tree already reveals each button's location, so the model doesn't have to go through the trouble of finding pixels. Go one step further, and the model doesn’t even need coordinates; it can pick a button by ID and let the harness click it. To test this, we built three setups, each building upon the last:

1.   Screenshots alone
2.   Adding an accessibility tree (clicking by coordinates)
3.   Adding clicks by element IDs

Every setup used the same agent on 172 OSWorld tasks, with one attempt per task, a 50-step limit and low reasoning effort, scored by OSWorld’s own graders.

The model runs in a loop where it first sees a screenshot and past actions, picks an action (click coordinates, type or press keys), and then looks at the changes. It’s the simplest way to give a model a computer, and the one most agents start with. OSWorld’s baseline agent supports it, and Anthropic [described its first computer use model](https://www.anthropic.com/news/developing-computer-use) as looking at screenshots and counting how many pixels to move the cursor.

We ran the same screenshot agent across seven OpenAI models:

| Model | Released | Screenshots only |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPT-4o | May 2024 | 10.5% |
| GPT-4.1 | Apr 2025 | 5.4% |
| GPT-5.2 | Dec 2025 | 15.8% |
| GPT-5.4 nano | Mar 2026 | 7.5% |
| GPT-5.5 | Apr 2026 | 67.7% |
| GPT-6 Luna | Sep 2026 | 59.2% |
| GPT-6.1 Sol | Sep 2026 | 83.8% |

On our 172 tasks, GPT-4.1 scored a mere 5.4% with screenshots alone, while the more recent GPT-6.1 Sol scored 83.8%. On the much harder OSWorld 2.0 offline set, OpenAI reports a score of [71.4% for GPT-6.1 Sol](https://x.com/OpenAIDevs/status/2104993086099398854) at maximum reasoning effort. The gap between the two models raised questions: do stronger models even need the tree, and can it help weaker ones catch up?

Here, the model sees the screenshot with an accessibility tree beside it. We were interested in the tree because it can just tell the model what’s there, like a button labeled “Save” and where it sits. The model still clicks by coordinates here. The tree lists each element's position and dimensions in pixels, so the model can work out where to click after doing the math. With the clicking kept constant, the only thing that changed was what the model saw.

Hover the tree or the screen.

Each line provides an element's position and size in pixels. The model has to turn these numbers into a click.

OSWorld runs on Linux, and so our agents read AT-SPI. The app's toolkit, such as GTK and Qt, describes what's on screen and passes on those descriptions to any program that asks for them, without prompting the user for permissions. Also, while testing, we realized that GIMP was missing from the tree until we added back an environment variable set at login.

In the evals, trees helped every model that struggled with screenshots. GPT-5.2 went from 15.8% with screenshots alone to 36.2% after the tree was added, and GPT-4.1 from 5.4% to 20.6%. On the other hand, stronger models barely moved. GPT-6.1 Sol got 82.7% when the tree was added, slightly lower than with screenshots alone (83.8%) and none of the three strongest models changed by a statistically significant amount.

Next, we gave each element in the tree an ID. The model can simply name the element it wants and the harness clicks it. This bypasses the problem of clicking the exact pixel.

Click the calculator. Your click stands in for the model’s coordinates, and it drifts a few pixels.

For weaker models, ID clicks boosted performance on top of the tree. GPT-5.2 went from 36.2% with the tree + coordinates to 52.8% when it clicked by ID, and GPT-4.1 from 20.6% to 29.3%. Put together, the tree and ID clicks more than tripled GPT-5.2’s score with screenshots alone (15.8%).

Some apps publish no tree at all. A canvas app like Figma publishes its toolbar buttons, but the canvas itself is just pixels, and a game like Doom is pixels from top to bottom. Even in apps with a good tree, some bugs only show on screen, like text that overflows its box. The screenshot covers all of these.

Code review catches bugs in the diff. Some bugs only exist when the software is running: a button that can’t be clicked, a label that runs off the edge of the window. Until now, catching those took a person opening the app and simulating the user flow. By writing more code and touching more of the UI than any team can check by hand, coding agents have made it hard for programmers to keep up.

That’s why we built computer use into [TREX](https://www.greptile.com/blog/trex-code-execution). It runs the changes in your pull request on an actual desktop and uses the app the way a person would, so you can see that the feature you asked for is the one that got built.

How TREX sees the screen came out of these experiments. It runs on the best models and relies on the screenshot at every step. It uses the accessibility tree to click by ID when it can, and coordinates when the tree doesn't have the element, like a canvas or a game.

How a model should see the screen depends on the model, so we'll rerun these experiments each time a new one comes out and update TREX when the answer changes.

When something breaks on screen, TREX catches it, and shows you what happened.

Try TREX on your next pull request.
