The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we're introducing more personally relevant responses, so it's easier to find just what you need.

Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to [Personal Intelligence](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/personal-intelligence-expansion/) in [AI Mode](http://g.ai/), with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search. These apps join Gmail, Calendar, and Photos in delivering even more tailored responses with your personal context.

*   **Get a clearer picture of your spending with Google Wallet:** By connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in both AI Mode and the [Gemini app](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/google-wallet-gemini-app/), you can map out your financial milestones and identify actionable ways to trim everyday spending. You can also maximize credit card benefits — like optimizing cash-back categories, travel perks, and reward points — based on your cards linked via Wallet. If you choose to connect your Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from your accounts; it can’t move, manage, or invest your money.
*   **Stay in your flow with Google Drive:** Sometimes the important information that you need to get started on a project or make a big decision can be scattered across your docs, sheets, or PDFs. With Google Drive connected in Personal Intelligence, you can get uniquely helpful responses that take all of that context into account and help you get started, like a personalized preparation plan ahead of tax season.
*   **Connect the dots between the Gemini app and Search:** In the coming weeks you can easily share context across the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search. So if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa. While you could already opt in to [connect your Search history](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/personal-intelligence/) to Personal Intelligence in the Gemini app, soon you can also opt in to securely connect your Gemini app to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next?
see all updates
After Nvidia’s board
accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO
, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on
Stephen A. Smith’s radio show
shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”
“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said,
floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook
as a potential CEO candidate.
It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was
working to grease the landing
for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they
voted unanimously to reinstate
him as CEO, president, and board director.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory
call to
CNBC
.
Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.
“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback”
Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump
said
he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per
The New York Times
, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly
dialed into
Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told
CNBC
on Monday.
News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had
assured stakeholders
on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility.
Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and
perhaps illegally
— extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on
CNBC
that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”
But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration.
The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a
direct report
, as well as an alleged
third affair
with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been
investigated for
a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he
reportedly
lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st.
The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its
announcement
Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation.
The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added.
Still, the reaction to Huang’s return reflects how small the chance of Huang’s return seemed before Trump’s efforts. Although Trump had previously
cast doubt
on multiple reports that Alice Huang was a spy,
The New York Times
reported
on Sunday that she “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year.” According to the
Times
, which cited multiple people with knowledge of US intelligence reports, Kang Wei — Alice Huang’s business partner and, by some reports, husband, who reportedly introduced her to the Nvidia CEO — worked with the same Chinese intelligence agency. But on Sunday evening, Trump still argued for Huang’s return and managed to continue flipping Nvidia’s board in his favor after a
weekend’s worth of efforts
.
“[I]ndefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible”
If the board maintained any hang-ups about bringing Huang back as CEO, Trump’s power over the executive branch — and the pressure he could exert with it — might have offered a compelling counterargument. The Securities and Exchange Commission had previously
opened an investigation
into whether Nvidia “misled investors,” according to
The Wall Street Journal
. But in a post on Truth Social Monday,
Trump said
that the attorney general “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Reached for comment, the DOJ did not provide an on-the-record response in line with
The Verge
’s editorial policy.
Key Democrats have indicated that both Nvidia and the Trump administration will be under fire when the new Congress is sworn in — and momentum has built behind GPU export controls, which Huang lobbied extensively to loosen. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said in a
post on X,
adding they’d work “on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.” Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)
called
the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible” and pledged to investigate “business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce.” He called for “traditional Republicans” to join in the effort.
“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a
statement
. “Jensen Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, “A real Congress will find out” whether Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had any alternative incentives for their role in Nvidia’s dealings. Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, called Trump’s intervention to bring back Huang “outrageous.” Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-TX), a member of the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees, which are interviewing Huang next week, said he wants to know how Trump stands to benefit from “personally champion[ing] Huang’s return.”
“We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO”
At closed-door hearings next week, Democrats say they intend to press Huang and the administration further, and several accused the administration of corruption. “We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC’s access to our most sensitive technology,” Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement to
The Verge
. The board’s decision is “outrageous,” said Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL), a member of the House Select Committee on China. “We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement, calling for Huang to testify publicly. “Reinstatement is no substitute for accountability,” Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), another China Committee member, said in a statement.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta also intends to continue an investigation into the company. “The reinstatement of Jensen Huang does not change the fact that the American people deserve to know what happened here — whether Nvidia misled investors and the public,” California Department of Justice spokesperson Elissa Perez said in a statement.
Last week, before Huang was reinstated, at least two Republican China hawks opposed the idea. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), a rumored potential presidential candidate, told reporters that he would not like to see Huang return to the top post, but would “defer to the board how they want to run their company. If it were me and a guy who just was caught up in a Chinese honeytrap — I think is the technical term for it — I don’t think that I would impose massive security concerns, not just for the company, but for American national security.”
While it was up to the board to decide whether to bring Huang back, Hawley said, “We in Congress ought to be concerned about the American national security implications and I think we should be looking into that.”
Huang “has a serious credibility problem”
House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) said on stage last week at the Aspen Cyber Summit in Washington, D.C., that Huang “has a serious credibility problem, and I don’t believe he would be as effective now as he was before.” His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment after Huang’s reinstatement

Justine Calma
is a senior science reporter covering energy and the environment with more than a decade of experience. She is also the host of
Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home
, a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals.
The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this”
To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations,
told
Politico
in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit.
Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change
rejected the deal that they saw as too weak
. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration
pulled the country out
of the Paris accord (twice).
With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some
environmental
and
humanitarian groups
called this year “the worst COP” ever.
To meet the Paris goals
, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside.
Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline
to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual
sustainability report
on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution.
Google’s
and
Microsoft’s
carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the I
nternational Energy Agency
.
Related
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
“That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells
The Verge
in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a
panel
on the challenges during the event.
In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could
increase 42 percent
by 2030 as energy companies
build more fossil fuel infrastructure
to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent
analysis
by the Sierra Club. Already,
hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark

articles.content:
Title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-shirudo/

Markdown Content:
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a [controlled test⁠(opens in a new window)](https://isovalent.com/blog/post/cisco-openai-shirudo/), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

## How Shirudo works

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:

*   **Live protection:** eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

*   **Defense at machine speed:** OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

*   **Trusted deployment:** Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

*   **Hardware-backed verification:** Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

The [Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window)](https://lpc.events/event/20/contributions/2437/) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to [apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4v2xA_NJHt0). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more [here⁠(opens in a new window)](https://isovalent.com/blog/post/cisco-openai-shirudo/).

## Rethinking infrastructure

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

## Building in the open

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing[Shirudo⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

*   **Try Shirudo:** Follow the[VM quickstart⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.shirudo.dev/start/quickstart.html) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

*   **Get hands-on:** Explore Shirudo through [Isovalent's self-guided lab⁠(opens in a new window)](https://labs.isovalent.com/#/lab/shirudo-getting-started).

*   **Join the technical deep dive:** Register for the [December 15 webinar⁠(opens in a new window)](https://isovalent.site/4t8Pjxc).

We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the[code on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo), read the[docs⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.shirudo.dev/index.html), and[let us know what you find⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.shirudo.dev/contribute/support.html).

Title: Kagi Mail is here (Public Beta)

URL Source: https://blog.kagi.com/kagi-mail-public-beta

Published Time: 2026-11-23T12:00:34.000Z

Markdown Content:
We are proud to announce something that our small team of very dedicated people at Kagi has been building for a long time – the **public beta of Kagi Mail**. A private email and calendar with a @kagimail.com address, or with your own domains.

If you’ve already swapped Google Search for Kagi and Chrome for Orion, your inbox is probably the last big piece of your digital life still at Google. Now you can move that too.

## Why we built it

_Does the world need another email service?_ We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: **technology should do its job and then get out of your way**.

For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.

[Kagi Mail](https://kagi.com/products/mail) also has to treat you the way Kagi Search and Orion do: no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.

**Already a Kagi member?**

Kagi Mail is included in **Ultimate**. Sign in with your Kagi account, and you’re set. AI features draw from your existing Allowance. On another plan, or no Kagi account yet? After the free 60-day trial, you can get Kagi Mail for $99/year (+ Sales Tax).

## How it works: A service and a client, on open standards

To deliver the experience we believe in, we built the full stack: hosting for your addresses and domains, plus the mail and calendar apps. It runs on open standards and open-source infrastructure (the Stalwart server, IMAP, JMAP, and CalDAV), so you can use Kagi’s apps or any compatible client you already like.

### The basics

*   A @kagimail.com address
*   Unlimited aliases
*   Unlimited domains
*   Built-in Calendar
*   50 GB of storage

### Intelligence

*   **Organize your mail in your own words.** Brief it the way you’d brief an assistant: “Label anything where beta users send product feedback. It might come from @kagimail.com, but use judgment.” You decide what permissions each rule gets (read the content, or skip the inbox).
*   **Inbox Highlights** show what needs you today, and learn from what you dismiss.
*   **Ask your inbox** in plain language and get direct answers with the source email, including text inside scanned PDFs and photos.
*   **Newsletter view** reads newsletters like a feed, out of the way of real mail.
*   **Responsible AI, with one switch to turn it all off.** You control [what AI is allowed to do and infer](https://help.kagi.com/kagi/why-kagi/ai-philosophy.html).

### Private by default

*   Tracking pixels and remote images are blocked or proxied, so senders can’t tell when or where you opened their mail.
*   Sender screening holds new senders until you approve them, so they never reach your inbox uninvited.
*   Suspicious senders trigger a phishing warning, while verified senders show their (BMI) logo.

**No ads, ever. No profiling, no selling, no sharing your data.**

### For teams and families

*   **Shared addresses on your domain** (team@, info@, family@): create an alias, then choose which people have access to it
*   Sign in through a social login, or your organization’s own identity provider (OIDC)
*   **Coming soon:** Shared mailboxes

### Kagi integration

*   Kagi Translate is built in
*   **Email Assistant:** Write to assistant@kagimail.com for answers about your mail (actions coming soon)
*   Proofread and translation included while you write emails

### For power users and developers

*   **Keyboard-first:** command palette, shortcuts, and search operators
*   Rule-based filtering with Sieve, no AI involved
*   MCP server with read access to your mail
*   Works with Apple Mail, Thunderbird, and any IMAP/JMAP/CalDAV client, with automatic setup

### What’s not here yet

We will keep adding new capabilities – here’s what to expect over the next few quarters.

| Feature | Target |
| --- | --- |
| Contacts and address book | Q1 2027 |
| Full Kagi Assistant integration | Q1 2027 |
| Native mobile apps | Q3 2027 |

Until the mobile apps arrive, use the mobile web app or any IMAP/JMAP client, such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird.

## Our “no lock-in” promise to you

Leaving Kagi Mail is as easy as joining it. Your mail, calendar, and workflows are yours, and you can export them at any time, through standard protocols and a one-click export experience. You’ll keep access to your mailbox for six months after leaving Kagi Mail. You can send and receive emails for the first 60 days, then read and export your mail with one click for the remaining four months. **We build an ecosystem so things work better together for those who want it, not to trap anyone**.

**We want Kagi Mail to be the first email account we’d create for our children.** We’re not there yet, but it is a high bar we hold ourselves to, and every feature in this beta is a step toward it: a calm, safe place to communicate, and a window onto an internet that treats you as a person, not a product who’s been tracked, targeted, and sold to.

**We can build it this way because of you.** Kagi has no ad business, and no one pushing us to monetize your inbox; you’re not a dataset for ads or AI. You are here because you believe the internet can be built differently. Thank you.

URL Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20031

Markdown Content:
[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.20031)[HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.20031v3)

> Abstract:We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% ->39.9%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

Title: Declare — a UI language for you and your AI

URL Source: https://davidtemkin.github.io/declarelang/

Markdown Content:
01

Expressive. And verifiable.

A calendar that zooms through time, a desktop with real windows: complete programs, each readable end to end and checked by the compiler. Open one, or edit it live in the browser you’re using.

1

Declare Calendar

Day, week, month and year views are one surface, zooming continuously; a view doesn’t switch so much as become the next one, and every motion can be interrupted. It runs on real data: drag an event to another day, and it’s moved.

568

lines of code, plus 228 of comments — four views, zoom, drag and edit

177 KB

over the wire, gzipped — app (structure, logic, styling) and runtime

0

lines typed by hand — human-designed and directed, built with AI

Run Declare Calendar →

View & edit source →

2

Declare Desktop

→

The acid test for a UI language: multiple applications, windows that drag, resize, layer and minimize into live thumbnails, a magnifying dock, menus that follow focus, and separately loaded apps running inside its windows. Elsewhere that is a project assembled from several libraries; here it is one program.

3529 lines — 2011 code, 939 comment · 264 KB over the wire · every pixel drawn from shapes, no image assets

View & edit source →

3

Declare Tracker

→

1,000,000 issues · search as you type · edit in place, with undo · not one line of virtualization code

1508 lines — 983 code, 251 comment · 194 KB over the wire, before its data · no dependencies

View & edit source →

And more:

Weather →

Market Map →

Birds →

To-do →

Asteroids →

02

Say what you mean. Exactly.

Declare was designed first for the people who make interfaces. Layout, motion, states, theming and drawing are the language itself, not libraries bolted on — so the experience you have in mind is something you can write down directly, and read back later as it was meant.

Rules

Data

Motion

Three things follow one value: the number, the bar’s length and its color. Click to change v — all three update together, because each is a relationship that stays true, not a step someone remembered to run.

LIVE · EDITABLE

Revert

40

click anywhere to change v

Your AI can write the code. Can it tell when it’s wrong?

In Declare, yes. A small language gets it started; these four tools let it catch its mistakes, fix them, and finish.

Start with context

One installable skill: the language, the library, the conventions, the working loop — nothing to reconstruct from a repository. And declare-help answers any name or error code on demand.

Correct, don’t guess

Every diagnostic names the broken rule and the valid rewrite. Try it: change textColor to color in the panel above and read what comes back.

Question the result

The Inspector can tell you or an agent why a live value is what it is, what it depends on, and what happens if you change it — live, in the running program, not guessed from source.

Prove the change

A formal six-rung ladder, from parse to pixels, is how an app is shown to be correct. Your AI climbs it one rung at a time, and every rung reports what it proved — and what it cannot see.

Measured: given the same brief, the same agent built a ticket-buying app twice. The Declare app was 1,279 lines to React’s 2,666, and its first build that ran passed all eleven hidden checks; React’s passed six. Single runs, not yet a benchmark — every run is in the repository.

The calendar above was built this way: human-designed and directed, built with AI, and kept honest by the compiler.
